title: Context: Caribbean Immigration & British Identity
description: Winsome Pinnock, the Windrush generation and the 1980s context behind Leave Taking.
content_html:
Winsome Pinnock and Leave Taking

Leave Taking (1987) by Winsome Pinnock is a play about a Caribbean-British family navigating questions of identity, belonging and cultural roots in 1984 London. For OCR, you study it as a modern drama text in Component 01 or 02. The play focuses on Enid Matthews, a Jamaican-born mother raising two daughters (Del and Viv) in England, and her complex relationship with Mai — an Obeah woman who represents the Caribbean spiritual traditions Enid has tried to leave behind.

Key Fact

Pinnock was one of the first Black British women playwrights to have work staged in major London theatres. Leave Taking draws on the Windrush generation experience — Caribbean immigrants who came to Britain seeking a better life but faced racism, cultural displacement and the challenge of raising children between two worlds.

Historical Context

After World War II, Britain actively recruited workers from the Caribbean. The British Nationality Act 1948 gave them the right to settle. The HMT Empire Windrush brought the first large group in 1948. By 1984, when the play is set, the children of these immigrants were growing up British but facing racism and questions about where they truly belonged. The 1981 Brixton riots and the 1971 Immigration Act form part of the backdrop to the racial tensions Enid's family navigates.

Pinnock is part of a tradition of Black British theatre that emerged in the 1980s, giving voice to experiences largely absent from mainstream stages. Leave Taking is significant because it centres Caribbean-British women's experiences — motherhood, cultural identity, generational conflict — rather than presenting them as secondary to male or white narratives. When the National Theatre produced the play in 1994, it was the first time a Black British woman's play had been staged there — a historic milestone. The 2018 Bush Theatre revival, directed by Madani Younis, introduced the play to a new generation.

The Play's Two Settings

Leave Taking is set in 1984 London and is structured as eight scenes — not two formal acts. The play has two physical settings: Enid's North London living room (Scenes 2–5) and Mai's Deptford bedsit (Scenes 1, 6, 7, 8). The play opens and closes at Mai's bedsit — the Caribbean spiritual space frames the entire action. This is structurally significant: the domestic English space is bracketed by the world of Obeah and Caribbean roots, suggesting that Enid's attempt to confine her family to English respectability is always surrounded by the heritage she tried to suppress.

Key Fact

Scene 1 takes place on Easter Monday, 1984, at Mai's Deptford bedsit. Enid brings both daughters there for a reading. Del stays behind when Enid and Viv leave. The play's final scene (Scene 8) also takes place at Mai's bedsit — where Del reads Enid's palm as Mai's spiritual successor. The Caribbean space opens and closes the play, framing the family's journey.

The first generation of Caribbean immigrants faced a painful dilemma: to survive in a racist Britain, many felt they had to suppress their cultural identity, language and spiritual practices. The cost of this strategy fell on the second generation, who grew up in England but felt culturally rootless. They were too English for Jamaica, but not fully accepted in England. Pinnock's play dramatises this dilemma through Enid (first generation) and her daughters Del and Viv (second generation). The tension between assimilation and cultural belonging is the engine of the entire play.

Context and Critical Reception

Understanding the social and historical context in which a play was written is essential for top-band exam responses. For Leave Taking, this means engaging with the experience of the Windrush generation and the particular challenges facing Black British women in the 1980s. Winsome Pinnock brings her own background to the play, writing from within a community whose stories had been largely absent from mainstream British theatre. The play's critical reception has grown over time: the 1994 National Theatre production was historic, and the 2018 Bush Theatre revival confirmed its status as a landmark text in British drama. When writing about the play, always connect the specific scene or character detail you are analysing to this broader context — explaining not just what Pinnock shows, but why she chose to show it.

practice_questions.text: How does Pinnock use the historical and social context of the Windrush generation in Leave Taking? [20 marks]
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (17–20): Perceptive analysis of how context shapes the play. Discusses Windrush migration, 1980s racism, the assimilation dilemma. Links context to specific character choices and Pinnock's dramatic purpose. AO3 integrated throughout.

Mid band (9–16): Clear discussion with some analysis of context's dramatic function.

Lower band (1–8): Describes context without linking to the play's methods.

practice_questions.text: Compare how Pinnock and the writer of the unseen text present the experience of feeling caught between two cultures. Consider language, form and structure. [20 marks]
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (17–20): Perceptive comparison. Analyses Pinnock's dual setting, code-switching dialogue, and layered title. Compares with the unseen text's methods. AO3 integrated.

Mid band (9–16): Clear comparison with some analysis.

Lower band (1–8): Limited comparison, mainly descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Explore how Pinnock's own background and the theatrical context of the 1980s influenced Leave Taking. [20 marks]
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (17–20): Analyses Pinnock as a Black British woman playwright in the 1980s. Discusses the absence of Caribbean-British women's stories from mainstream theatre, the National Theatre 1994 milestone, and the 2018 revival. Links to Pinnock's centring of women's experiences.

Mid band (9–16): Clear discussion with relevant examples.

Lower band (1–8): Basic context statements.

practice_questions.text: Compare how Pinnock and the writer of the unseen text present the relationship between place and identity. Consider language, form and structure. [20 marks]
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (17–20): Perceptive comparison. Analyses Pinnock's two physical settings as embodying different identities. The structural significance of opening and closing at Mai's bedsit. Compares with the unseen text.

Mid band (9–16): Clear comparison.

Lower band (1–8): Limited comparison.

practice_questions.text: How does Pinnock present the idea that cultural heritage cannot be permanently suppressed? [20 marks]
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (17–20): Analyses Del's pull towards Mai, Enid's emotional collapse after her mother's death (Scene 3), Viv's rejection of Eurocentric education. How Pinnock structures the play so Caribbean heritage reasserts itself. Links to Windrush experience.

Mid band (9–16): Clear discussion with evidence.

Lower band (1–8): Basic identification.

practice_questions.text: 'Leave Taking argues that where you come from is more powerful than where you live.' How far do you agree? [20 marks]
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (17–20): Evaluative. Agrees: play opens and closes at Caribbean spiritual space; Del's heritage ultimately defines her arc. Complicates: the resolution is about holding both, not choosing; Viv is genuinely English as well as Jamaican. Nuanced conclusion.

Mid band (9–16): Clear argument with evidence.

Lower band (1–8): Simple agreement.

knowledge_checks.q: In what year is Leave Taking set?
Where does the play both open and close?
Leave Taking is structured as _____ scenes, not two formal acts.
The 1994 National Theatre production was historic because it was the first play by a _____ to be staged there.
Match each setting to the scenes it appears in:
right: Scenes 1, 6, 7, 8 — the play opens and closes here

flashcard_questions.q: Who wrote Leave Taking and when was it first performed?
flashcard_questions.a: Winsome Pinnock — first performed at Liverpool Playhouse Studio in 1987.
Caribbean immigrants who came to Britain between 1948 and 1971 following the British Nationality Act 1948.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the two physical settings in Leave Taking?
flashcard_questions.a: Enid's North London living room (Scenes 2–5) and Mai's Deptford bedsit (Scenes 1, 6, 7, 8).

flashcard_questions.q: Why is it significant that the play opens and closes at Mai's bedsit?
flashcard_questions.a: The Caribbean spiritual space frames the whole action — heritage cannot be suppressed despite Enid's efforts.

flashcard_questions.q: In what year is Leave Taking set, and on what day does it open?
flashcard_questions.a: 1984 — the first scene takes place on Easter Monday.
Eight scenes — not two formal acts.

flashcard_questions.q: What historic milestone did Leave Taking achieve at the National Theatre in 1994?
flashcard_questions.a: It was the first play by a Black British woman to be staged at the National Theatre.

flashcard_questions.q: What dilemma did first-generation Caribbean immigrants face?
flashcard_questions.a: To survive racism, many suppressed their cultural identity — but this left their English-born children culturally rootless.
A Caribbean folk spiritual practice rooted in West African traditions, practised by Mai in the play.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the title 'Leave Taking' mean thematically?
flashcard_questions.a: Multiple departures: Enid leaving Jamaica, the daughters leaving Enid's values, and the family leaving shame behind.

glossary_terms.definition: A person's sense of who they are, shaped by culture, heritage and experience.
A practitioner of folk magic and spiritual healing in Caribbean culture.
Caribbean people who migrated to Britain between 1948 and 1971, recruited as Commonwealth citizens to help rebuild post-war Britain.
Law granting British citizenship to Commonwealth residents, enabling Caribbean migration to Britain.
Adopting the cultural norms of the dominant society, often at the expense of one's own heritage.
Women of Caribbean descent living in Britain, whose experiences Pinnock centres in Leave Taking.
British law that restricted the rights of Commonwealth citizens to settle in the UK, ending the open migration of the Windrush era.

exam_tip_html: When writing about Context: Caribbean Immigration & British Identity, focus your analysis on the specific dramatic and structural choices the playwright makes. Examiners reward responses that connect language details to wider themes, and that show understanding of the social and historical context in which the play was written. Avoid retelling the plot — instead, explain the effect of specific techniques on the audience.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • This lesson has covered the key ideas and dramatic techniques relevant to Context: Caribbean Immigration & British Identity. Make sure you can discuss specific examples from the text, link techniques to themes, and embed relevant context in your analysis.
